summary:
Moon to Mars is a free, browser-based game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 10 days. Players manage Air, Power and Shield, plus food and crew health, and every action has a cost, so saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow.
 Space education for kids is often too simple to show real trade-offs, or too complex to hold their attention. Astro Quest turns those trade-offs into play. A daily space weather forecast built from NASA DONKI solar storm data decides how dangerous each day is. Radiation, temperature and power figures come from NASA sources such as Curiosity RAD, LRO Diviner and Opportunity rover data. Every real value shows its source and a LIVE or ARCHIVED badge, and estimates are labeled.
 Young learners rarely see the decisions behind space missions, only the outcomes. Astro Quest lets them feel those choices, and each day ends with a "What happened and why?" card that explains the result. It needs no download or account.
details:
What it does and how it works: Astro Quest: Moon to Mars is a free, browser-based game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 10 days. Players manage Air, Power and Shield, plus food and crew health. Every action has a cost, so saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow. Each day, a space weather forecast built from NASA DONKI solar storm data (live when available, otherwise archived) decides how dangerous the day is. A "What happened and why?" card then explains the result and names the NASA source.

Benefits: Kids learn real engineering trade-offs through play, not just facts. It needs no download or account, so it works in classrooms and at home. Teachers also get a lesson guide and discussion questions.

Intended impact: We want a child to finish a game understanding one real constraint of deep space survival. We hope it builds problem-solving and decision-making skills and sparks interest in space science.

Tools used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with unit tests, hosted as a static website. Data came from NASA DONKI, LRO Diviner, Curiosity RAD, the Chang'E-4 lander, Opportunity rover figures and NASA life support figures. We also used AI tools (Antigravity IDE and Claude) to help write code, draft text and cross-check figures. Our team reviewed and tested the results.

Creativity: Players can replay real storms (October 2003 and May 2024), so every game plays out differently. Moon and Mars video backgrounds react to the storm level, Mars adds a real communication delay, and an astronaut guide named Nova explains each choice in plain language. Failure is shown as learning, not punishment.

Factors we considered: age-appropriate language, honest LIVE or ARCHIVED labels, a source tag on every real value, no free choices, and keeping the game to three main resources so young players aren't overwhelmed.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI Space Weather Database (solar flares and storms)
NASA Curiosity Rover (RAD radiation measurements on Mars)
NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (Diviner Moon temperatures)
NASA Mars Exploration Rovers (Opportunity dust storm power data)
projectRefs: Chang'E-4 lander radiation measurements on the Moon (Science Advances)
Planetary Society: Opportunity and the 2018 dust storm
